lesson.title: Introdução ao Processamento de Linguagem Natural
lesson.description: O objetivo deste encontro é apresentar ao estudante os conceitos essenciais para o Processamento de Linguagem Natural. Quais são os conceitos principais e em quais áreas ele pode ser aplicado. Com o término da instrução, os estudantes deverão ser capazes de apresentar esses conceitos e iniciar o processo de familiarização das tecnologias empregadas.
related_labels: Introdução ao Processamento de Linguagem Natural
Processamento de texto, métricas e técnicas

before_phase4_candidates.label: Bash as Command Language Interpreter
before_phase4_candidates.description: Bash is a shell that interprets commands typed by the user to interact with the operating system.
coverage_criteria: Define Bash and explain its role as a command-language interpreter.
Identify that typing a command in the terminal and pressing enter causes the shell to interpret and execute that command.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video explicitly introduces Bash as a command language interpreter for interacting with the computer from the command line.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a foundational concept that can be verified by asking the student to define Bash or explain what happens when a command is entered.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Shell as Kernel Wrapper
before_phase4_candidates.description: The shell surrounds the operating system kernel, hiding its complexity and allowing programmers to execute tasks (data access, file creation) with simple commands.
coverage_criteria: Explain why the shell is considered a 'shell' around the kernel.
Describe how the shell simplifies access to system functionality like file management.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video describes the shell as 'surrounding the operating system kernel to hide its intricate details' and demonstrates basic commands like touch and cat.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: The concept is small enough to be tested by asking the student to contrast the shell's role with the kernel's complexity.

before_phase4_candidates.label: History of Unix Shells
before_phase4_candidates.description: Unix shells evolved from the Thompson shell (1971) by Ken Thompson, to the Bourne shell by Stephen Bourne (1979), and finally to Bash (Bourne-Again Shell) by Brian Fox in 1989.
coverage_criteria: Name the three major shells in chronological order and their creators.
Explain why Bash is called the Bourne-Again Shell.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video provides a timeline of shell development, showing images and dates for Thompson, Bourne, and Bash.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This historical overview is a self-contained piece of knowledge that can be assessed with a few recall questions.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Bash as Default Unix Shell
before_phase4_candidates.description: On most Unix-like systems such as macOS and Linux distributions, Bash is the default shell when opening a terminal, providing a prompt for command input.
coverage_criteria: State that Bash is the default shell on many Unix systems.
Recognize the terminal prompt as the Bash shell waiting for commands.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video mentions that when you open the terminal on a Unix machine like macOS and most Linux distros, the default shell is usually Bash.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This fact can be verified with a simple yes/no or multiple-choice question, making it an appropriately granular candidate.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Checking Current Shell with `which $SHELL`
before_phase4_candidates.description: The command `which $SHELL` reveals the full path of the current shell executable (e.g., `/usr/bin/bash`), indicating whether Bash is running.
coverage_criteria: Execute `which $SHELL` in a terminal and interpret the output.
Explain that the shell is an application located in the binaries directory.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video demonstrates the command `which $SHELL` and its output `/usr/bin/bash` to verify that Bash is the running shell.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a single command that can be practiced and checked easily, representing a minimal checkable skill.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Bash as a Scripting Language
before_phase4_candidates.description: Bash is not only an interactive shell but also a programming language that allows writing scripts to automate command-line tasks.
coverage_criteria: Explain that Bash scripts automate sequences of commands.
Identify that a Bash script is a file containing bash commands that can be executed.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video states that Bash is also a programming language that allows us to write scripts, automating manual commands.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept distinguishes Bash's dual nature and can be assessed with a single explanation question.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Bash Startup Files (.bash_profile and .bashrc)
before_phase4_candidates.description: When a Bash session starts, it automatically executes configuration files (typically `.bash_profile` or `.bashrc` in the home directory) to customize the shell environment.
coverage_criteria: Explain the purpose of startup scripts.
Identify that .bash_profile or .bashrc are used to set up aliases, environment variables, and prompt appearance.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video mentions that launching the shell runs a startup script defined in .bash_profile or .bashrc, and shows a customized prompt and git status as an example of customization.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This single configuration concept can be verified by asking where startup settings are stored and what they do.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Creating a Bash Script File
before_phase4_candidates.description: A Bash script is a plain text file (often with a `.sh` extension), starting with a shebang (`#!/usr/bin/bash`) that specifies the interpreter, followed by commands executed sequentially.
coverage_criteria: Write a script file with a shebang line and at least one command.
Explain the purpose of the shebang.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video demonstrates creating a script named beerme.sh, adding a shebang, and using echo, with the explanation that the first line should be the shebang followed by the path to the application.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This captures the minimal structure of a Bash script, which is a fundamental skill that can be tested with a short coding task.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Declaring and Using Variables in Bash
before_phase4_candidates.description: Variables in Bash are assigned with uppercase names and no spaces around `=` (e.g., `GREET="Hello"`) and are referenced by prefixing the name with `$` (e.g., `echo $GREET`).
coverage_criteria: Declare a variable in a Bash script.
Print the value of a variable using `$`.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video shows a variable `GREET="Howdy Partner"` and its use with `echo $GREET`, explicitly stating the rule: name in all caps, followed by equal sign, then reference with dollar sign.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Variable usage is a basic building block of scripting that can be validated with a simple exercise.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Executing a Bash Script
before_phase4_candidates.description: A Bash script is run by typing its path, e.g., `./script.sh`, from the command line (assuming the file has execute permissions).
coverage_criteria: Execute a script located in the current directory using `./scriptname.sh`.
Explain that `./` refers to the current directory.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video runs the script by typing `./beerme.sh` into the shell, demonstrating the execution method.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a single operational step that can be verified by asking the student to run a given script.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Using Positional Arguments ($1, $2, …)
before_phase4_candidates.description: When a script is invoked with arguments, those arguments are automatically available inside the script as $1, $2, etc., representing the first, second, etc. arguments.
coverage_criteria: Write a script that uses $1 and $2 to access passed arguments.
Explain that $0 typically contains the script name.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video demonstrates passing arguments `name age` and accessing them with `$1` and `$2` in the script.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Positional argument handling is a specific pattern in Bash scripting that can be assessed by having the student write or modify a script that uses them.

before_phase4_candidates.label: User Input with `read` and Loops
before_phase4_candidates.description: The `read -p` command prompts for user input; constructs like `while true; do ... done` and `case` statements enable interactive looping and decision-making.
coverage_criteria: Write a script that repeatedly prompts the user using a while loop and read -p.
Use a case statement to branch on user responses, including options for yes/no.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video shows a script with `while true; do read -p ...; case $reply in [Yy]* ... esac; done` to ask for user confirmation.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This composite skill involves a few interrelated commands, still checkable with a focused coding exercise.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Conditional `if` Statements in Bash
before_phase4_candidates.description: Bash supports `if` statements with comparison operators (e.g., `-lt`, `-gt`, `-eq`); the syntax is `if [ condition ]; then ... else ... fi`.
coverage_criteria: Write an if statement that compares two numbers.
Explain the syntax of an if-fi block and the use of `-lt`.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video shows `if [ $2 -lt 21 ]; then echo "You are too young..." else fi` to implement conditional logic based on age.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Conditional logic is a fundamental programming construct; this candidate focuses specifically on its Bash syntax, making it a well-scoped checkable item.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Running Commands in the Background
before_phase4_candidates.description: Appending an ampersand (`&`) to a command runs it asynchronously in the background, allowing multiple long-running processes to run concurrently.
coverage_criteria: Demonstrate running a command in the background using `&`.
Explain that the shell prompt returns immediately while the command runs.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The video shows multiple commands like `long_process &` to illustrate background execution, stating that adding an ampersand after a command runs it in the background.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a single shell feature that can be demonstrated with a short command, making it a concise checkable concept.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Defining functions with def, colon, and indentation
before_phase4_candidates.description: Python functions are defined using the def keyword followed by a name and parentheses. A colon indicates the start of the function body, which is delimited by consistent indentation (tabs or spaces), not curly braces.

before_phase4_candidates.label: List slicing in Python
before_phase4_candidates.description: Slicing allows extracting a sublist using the colon operator: list[start:end]. Omitting start or end takes from the beginning or until the end. Negative indices can be used in slices.

Can identify the need to re-run dependent cells after a change.

before_phase4_candidates.label: f-string formatting in Python
before_phase4_candidates.description: Using f-strings (formatted string literals) to embed variables and expressions directly within string literals for output.

before_phase4_candidates.label: Embedding variables in strings

reconciled_candidates.label: Natural Language Processing (NLP) Definition
reconciled_candidates.description: NLP is a branch of artificial intelligence that enables machines to read, understand, and derive meaning from human languages, combining linguistics and computer science.
coverage_criteria: Can define NLP and list its two foundational fields: linguistics and computer science.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: The definition of NLP is a foundational concept that stands alone.

reconciled_candidates.label: NLP Applications: Autocorrect and Plagiarism Checking
reconciled_candidates.description: Everyday NLP applications include autocorrect for spelling and plagiarism checkers that scan for duplicate content, saving time and effort.
coverage_criteria: Can list and describe two common NLP applications.

reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: These two applications are concrete examples of NLP in daily life, forming a distinct teachable concept.

reconciled_candidates.label: Segmentation
reconciled_candidates.description: Segmentation is the process of breaking a document into its constituent sentences using punctuation marks like full stops and commas.
coverage_criteria: Can define segmentation and identify sentence boundaries in a given text.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Segmentation is a clear, standalone preprocessing step in NLP.

reconciled_candidates.label: Tokenization
reconciled_candidates.description: Tokenization is the process of breaking sentences into individual words (tokens), often removing non-essential stop words to speed up processing.
coverage_criteria: Can define tokenization and list examples of tokens from a sentence.
Can explain why stop words are removed during tokenization.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Tokenization is a fundamental NLP step, and including stop words makes it a single checkable concept about word-level processing.

reconciled_candidates.label: Stop Words
reconciled_candidates.description: Stop words are common words like 'are', 'the', and 'in' that add little meaning to a statement and are removed to improve processing efficiency.
coverage_criteria: Can define stop words and identify them in a given sentence.
Can explain why stop words are removed in NLP preprocessing.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Stop words is a small, checkable concept that is a common optimization in NLP pipelines.

reconciled_candidates.label: Stemming
reconciled_candidates.description: Stemming is the process of reducing words to their root form by removing prefixes and suffixes, e.g., 'skipping' → 'skip'.
coverage_criteria: Can define stemming and provide examples of stemming transformations.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Stemming is a single normalization technique that can be tested by applying it to new words.

reconciled_candidates.label: Lemmatization
reconciled_candidates.description: Lemmatization is the process of reducing words to their dictionary base form (lemma) considering tense, mood, gender, etc., e.g., 'am', 'are', 'is' → 'be'.
coverage_criteria: Can define lemmatization and contrast it with stemming.
Can provide examples of lemmatization transformations.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: Lemmatization is distinct from stemming and requires understanding of dictionary forms.

reconciled_candidates.label: Part-of-Speech Tagging
reconciled_candidates.description: Part-of-speech (POS) tagging is the process of labeling each word in a sentence with its grammatical category, such as noun, verb, article, etc.
coverage_criteria: Can define POS tagging and identify parts of speech in a sample sentence.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: POS tagging is a core NLP annotation task that can be taught and tested in isolation.

reconciled_candidates.label: Named Entity Tagging
reconciled_candidates.description: Named entity tagging (NER) is the process of identifying and flagging names of people, organizations, locations, movies, etc., in a text.
coverage_criteria: Can define named entity tagging and recognize named entities in a given text.
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: NER is a distinct NLP task that can be assessed by asking students to highlight named entities.

reconciled_candidates.label: Machine Learning in NLP
reconciled_candidates.description: After preprocessing, machine learning algorithms like Naive Bayes are used to teach models human sentiment and speech patterns.
coverage_criteria: Can explain the role of machine learning in NLP and give an example algorithm (Naive Bayes).
reconciled_candidates.merge_rationale: The use of ML in NLP is a key concept that bridges preprocessing to applications.
